claim: Dentate neural stem cells produce neurons throughout life in mammals.
source: Dentate neural stem cells produce neurons throughout life in mammals.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about dentate neural stem cells.

claim: Sonic hedgehog (Shh) is critical for maintenance of dentate neural stem cells.
source: Sonic hedgehog (Shh) is critical for maintenance of these cells
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the manuscript and represents established knowledge.

claim: The perinatal source of Shh for dentate stem cells is enigmatic.
source: however, the perinatal source of Shh is enigmatic.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Hair follicles (HFs) expand perinatally in temporal concordance with the proliferation of Shh-responding dentate stem cells.
source: we examined the role of Shh expressed by hair follicles (HFs) that expand perinatally in temporal concordance with the proliferation of Shh-responding dentate stem cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the temporal analysis presented in the study.

claim: Specific inhibition of Shh from HFs hindered development of Shh-responding dentate stem cells.
source: Specific inhibition of Shh from HFs or from epithelial sources in general hindered development of Shh-responding dentate stem cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data using conditional knockout mice.

claim: Specific inhibition of Shh from epithelial sources in general hindered development of Shh-responding dentate stem cells.
source: Specific inhibition of Shh from HFs or from epithelial sources in general hindered development of Shh-responding dentate stem cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data using conditional knockout mice.

claim: The blood–brain barrier (BBB) of the perinatal dentate gyrus (DG) is leaky.
source: We also found that the blood–brain barrier (BBB) of the perinatal dentate gyrus (DG) is leaky with stem cells in the dentate exposed to blood-born factors.
evidence: This finding is supported by dye perfusion experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: Stem cells in the perinatal dentate are exposed to blood-born factors.
source: We also found that the blood–brain barrier (BBB) of the perinatal dentate gyrus (DG) is leaky with stem cells in the dentate exposed to blood-born factors.
evidence: This is inferred from the leaky BBB data presented in the study.

claim: Platelets contain epithelial Shh.
source: we found that platelets contain epithelial Shh
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and Western blot data of platelets.

claim: Platelets provide Shh to the perinatal DG.
source: we found that platelets contain epithelial Shh, provide Shh to the perinatal DG
evidence: This is supported by the presence of Shh-containing platelets in the dentate vasculature.

claim: Inhibition of platelet generation reduced hedgehog-responsive dentate stem cells.
source: inhibition of platelet generation reduced hedgehog-responsive dentate stem cells.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using Nfe2 knockout mice that fail to produce platelets.

claim: Stem cell niches in the adult dentate subgranular zone are established primarily by Sonic hedgehog (Shh)-responsive radial glial cells.
source: Stem cell niches in the adult dentate subgranular zone are established primarily by Sonic hedgehog (Shh)-responsive radial glial cells, which appear at embryonic day (E) 17 in mice (Ahn and Joyner, 2005; Li et al., 2013; Li and Pleasure, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Shh-responsive radial glial cells appear at embryonic day (E) 17 in mice.
source: Stem cell niches in the adult dentate subgranular zone are established primarily by Sonic hedgehog (Shh)-responsive radial glial cells, which appear at embryonic day (E) 17 in mice (Ahn and Joyner, 2005; Li et al., 2013; Li and Pleasure, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: In the adult, Shh plays a crucial role in maintaining the dentate stem cell niche and driving neurogenesis.
source: In the adult, Shh plays a crucial role in maintaining the dentate stem cell niche and driving neurogenesis (Machold et al., 2003; Ahn and Joyner, 2005; Han et al., 2008; Favaro et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Starting at the end of the first week of life in mice, Shh is provided locally by cells in the dentate hilus.
source: Starting at the end of the first week of life in mice, Shh is provided locally by cells in the dentate hilus (Li et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Shh-expressing cells are not present in the DG when dentate stem cells first appear.
source: however, Shh-expressing cells are not present in the DG when dentate stem cells first appear (Ahn and Joyner, 2005; Garcia et al., 2010; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: At earlier embryonic stages, the Shh ligand is produced by the amygdala and supplied to the adjacent ventral dentate neuroepithelium.
source: Our previous work showed that Shh from outside the dorsal forebrain is crucial for the establishment of the dentate stem cells in the dentate, and that at earlier embryonic stages, the Shh ligand is produced by the amygdala and supplied to the adjacent ventral dentate neuroepithelium and these stem cells then migrate to populate both the temporal and septal dentate just before birth in mice (at E17.5–18.5) (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Dentate stem cells migrate to populate both the temporal and septal dentate just before birth in mice (at E17.5–18.5).
source: Our previous work showed that Shh from outside the dorsal forebrain is crucial for the establishment of the dentate stem cells in the dentate, and that at earlier embryonic stages, the Shh ligand is produced by the amygdala and supplied to the adjacent ventral dentate neuroepithelium and these stem cells then migrate to populate both the temporal and septal dentate just before birth in mice (at E17.5–18.5) (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Postnatal dentate stem cells require Shh signaling to maintain stemness and division.
source: Since the postnatal dentate stem cells require Shh signaling to maintain stemness and division (Ahn and Joyner, 2005; Choe and Pleasure, 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Hair follicles are small structures stocked with cells producing factors such as platelet-derived growth factors (Pdgfs) and Shh.
source: hair follicles (HFs), each of which is a small structure stocked with cells producing factors such as platelet-derived growth factors (Pdgfs) and Shh (St-Jacques et al., 1998; Chiang et al., 1999; Karlsson et al., 1999; Fuchs, 2007; Blanpain and Fuchs, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The perinatal interaction of the epithelial and dermal mesenchymal cells establishes the stem cell niche for the HFs through crosstalk of a variety of signaling molecules.
source: The perinatal interaction of the epithelial and dermal mesenchymal cells establishes the stem cell niche for the HFs through crosstalk of a variety of signaling molecules (Rendl et al., 2005; Nowak et al., 2008)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: The development of HFs exposes new morphogens to nearby stem cell niches including mesenchymal stem cells and hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs).
source: the development of HFs exposes new morphogens to nearby stem cell niches including mesenchymal stem cells and hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs).
evidence: This is an inference based on the proximity and developmental timing of HFs and stem cell niches.

claim: Adult HSC niches form from embryonic HSCs that transiently reside in the liver by migration of the stem cells into the bone marrow.
source: Adult HSC niches form from embryonic HSCs that transiently reside in the liver by migration of the stem cells into the bone marrow.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HSC development.

claim: During late embryonic development, the skull is an active site for hematopoiesis, temporally coinciding with neurogenesis in the cortex.
source: During late embryonic development, the skull is an active site for hematopoiesis, temporally coinciding with neurogenesis in the cortex (Medvinsky et al., 2011; Li et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Bone marrow mesenchymal cells play a critical role of recruiting HSCs from the circulation by secreting Cxcl12.
source: bone marrow mesenchymal cells play a critical role of recruiting HSCs from the circulation by secreting Cxcl12, a critical homing signal for HSCs (Méndez-Ferrer and Frenette, 2007; Lo Celso et al., 2009; Méndez-Ferrer et al., 2010; Greenbaum et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cxcl12 is a critical homing signal for HSCs.
source: bone marrow mesenchymal cells play a critical role of recruiting HSCs from the circulation by secreting Cxcl12, a critical homing signal for HSCs (Méndez-Ferrer and Frenette, 2007; Lo Celso et al., 2009; Méndez-Ferrer et al., 2010; Greenbaum et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Osteoblastic cells in the skull niche control hematopoiesis including megakaryopoiesis in the context of skeletal homeostasis.
source: Thus, the osteoblastic cells in the skull niche control hematopoiesis including megakaryopoiesis in the context of skeletal homeostasis (Pallotta et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Megakaryocytes produce bone matrix components, cytokines and growth factors.
source: Megakaryocytes, one of the HSC lineages, produce bone matrix components, cytokines and growth factors
evidence: This is established knowledge about megakaryocyte function.

claim: Gata1 and Nfe2 knockout mice fail to release platelets from megakaryocytes and have abnormal bone mass.
source: mutant mice, which fail to release platelets from megakaryocytes such as Gata1 and Nfe2 knockout mice have abnormal bone mass (Kacena et al., 2004, 2005, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Activation of platelets leads to release of contents including Tgfβ1.
source: Activation of platelets leads to release of contents including Tgfβ1
evidence: This is established knowledge about platelet function.

claim: T lymphocytes shed microvesicles containing Shh.
source: T lymphocytes shed microvesicles containing Shh and Shh anchored in the microvesicles is functionally active in new blood vessel formation (Agouni et al., 2007; Soleti and Martinez, 2009; Benameur et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Shh anchored in microvesicles is functionally active in new blood vessel formation.
source: T lymphocytes shed microvesicles containing Shh and Shh anchored in the microvesicles is functionally active in new blood vessel formation (Agouni et al., 2007; Soleti and Martinez, 2009; Benameur et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: HFs in the head skin are established perinatally, coinciding with expansion of calvarial and dermal mesenchymal cells covering the developing brain.
source: HFs in the head skin are established perinatally, coinciding with expansion of calvarial and dermal mesenchymal cells covering the developing brain.
evidence: This is a temporal correlation observed in the study.

claim: The blood–brain barrier (BBB) matures as early as embryonic day (E) 15.5 in most forebrain areas.
source: The blood–brain barrier (BBB) matures as early as embryonic day (E) 15.5 in most forebrain areas (Daneman et al., 2010)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: The BBB in the DG matures postnatally.
source: The blood–brain barrier (BBB) matures as early as embryonic day (E) 15.5 in most forebrain areas (Daneman et al., 2010) except for a few areas, including the DG where the BBB matures postnatally.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: GFP + hedgehog-responding cells were obvious in the forming HFs of the dermis at E15.5 in Gli1-GFP transgenic mice.
source: The GFP + hedgehog-responding cells of a Gli1-GFP GENSAT transgenic mouse line were obvious in the forming HFs (Figure 1A, arrow heads) of the dermis at E15.5
evidence: This is directly observed in Figure 1A showing GFP expression in HFs.

claim: Calvarial bones showed GFP expression at later ages in Gli1-GFP transgenic mice.
source: The GFP + hedgehog-responding cells of a Gli1-GFP GENSAT transgenic mouse line were obvious in the forming HFs (Figure 1A, arrow heads) of the dermis at E15.5 when the dermal mesenchymal cells condense before the appearance of calvarial bones, which showed GFP expression at later ages (Figure 1A, red arrows).
evidence: This is observed in Figure 1A showing temporal progression of GFP expression.

claim: From E17.5 onward, the DG showed GFP + dentate progenitors and their descendants in Gli1-GFP mice.
source: From E17.5 onward, the DG showed GFP + dentate progenitors and their descendants (Figure 1A, yellow arrows).
evidence: This is directly observed in Figure 1A.

claim: Despite the expansion of dentate Gli1-GFP + cells, the expression of Shh was not detected in the dorsal cortex.
source: Despite the expansion of dentate Gli1-GFP + cells, the expression of Shh, however, was not detected in the dorsal cortex.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data for Shh expression.

claim: Perinatally, Shh expression was restricted in the ventral forebrain such as around the third ventricle and in the entorhinal cortex.
source: Perinatally, Shh expression was rather restricted in the ventral forebrain such as around the third ventricle and in the entorhinal cortex (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown by in situ hybridization in Figure 1B.

claim: The HFs, expanding dramatically after E17.5, were the geographically closest Shh-expressing cells to the DG when examined using the perinatal mouse head.
source: Interestingly, the HFs, expanding dramatically after E17.5, were the geographically closest Shh-expressing cells to the DG when examined using the perinatal mouse head (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on anatomical analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Krt14-Cre;Shhflx/flx mutants showed loss of Ptch1 expression in the skin.
source: The Krt14-Cre;Shhflx/flx mutants showed loss of Ptch1, a downstream target gene of hedgehog signaling, and Shh expression in the skin
evidence: This is shown by in situ hybridization in Figure 2A.

claim: Krt14-Cre;Shhflx/flx mutants showed loss of Shh expression in the skin.
source: The Krt14-Cre;Shhflx/flx mutants showed loss of Ptch1, a downstream target gene of hedgehog signaling, and Shh expression in the skin
evidence: This is shown by in situ hybridization in Figure 2A.

claim: Shh expression in the ventral forebrain was unaffected in Krt14-Cre;Shhflx/flx mutants.
source: The Krt14-Cre;Shhflx/flx mutants showed loss of Ptch1, a downstream target gene of hedgehog signaling, and Shh expression in the skin; however, Shh expression in the ventral forebrain was unaffected (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Prox1 staining showed more restricted localization of neurons in the upper blade of the Krt14-Cre;Shhflx/flx mutant DG.
source: Prox1 staining of the dentate granule neurons showed more restricted localization of neurons in the upper blade of the mutant DG (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B by Prox1 staining.

claim: Msx2-Cre;Shhflx/flx mutants survived to adulthood showing diminished epidermal Shh expression.
source: By utilizing an Msx2-Cre expressed in the skin area covering the forebrain (Choe et al., 2012), we generated conditional mutants that survived to adulthood showing diminished epidermal Shh expression.
evidence: This is based on experimental observation of mutant survival and Shh expression analysis.

claim: Msx2-Cre;Shhflx/flx mutants showed decreased numbers of dentate progenitors labeled by Ki67 at E16.5 and P3.
source: As observed in Krt14-Cre;Shhflx/flx mutants, the Msx2-Cre;Shhflx/flx mutants also showed decreased numbers of dentate progenitors labeled by Ki67 that coincided with the appearance of hedgehog-responsive dentate progenitors (Figure 3A,A′,B,B′).
evidence: This is shown and quantified in Figure 3A′ and B′.

claim: One hour BrdU labeling at P3 confirmed the diminished cell proliferation to one third of normal in the Msx2-Cre;Shhflx/flx mutant dentate.
source: One hour BrdU labeling at P3 confirmed the diminished cell proliferation to one third of normal in the mutant dentate (Figure 3C,C′).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 3C′ showing BrdU+ cell counts.

claim: Reduction of Shh expression was maintained in the skin of Msx2-Cre;Shhflx/flx mutants at P3.
source: Reduction of Shh expression was maintained in the skin; however, Shh + cells in the dorsal forebrain started to appear at P3 including in the hippocampal hilus (Figure 3D) (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is shown by in situ hybridization in Figure 3D.

claim: Shh + cells in the dorsal forebrain started to appear at P3 including in the hippocampal hilus.
source: Reduction of Shh expression was maintained in the skin; however, Shh + cells in the dorsal forebrain started to appear at P3 including in the hippocampal hilus (Figure 3D) (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and supported by citation.

claim: BrdU + dividing cells in the cortex did not show a significant difference between Msx2-Cre;Shhflx/flx mutants and controls at E17.5 and P1.
source: The BrdU + dividing cells in the cortex did not show a significant difference at both time points (Figure 3E,E′,E″).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 3E″ showing no significant difference.

claim: Shh from the HFs selectively affects dentate progenitors.
source: This result supports the idea that Shh from the HFs selectively affects dentate progenitors.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective effect on dentate but not cortical progenitors.

claim: At P3, the Msx2-Cre;Shhflx/flx;Ptch1-LacZ mutants showed a third of the X-gal stained cells in the dentate compared to their heterozygous littermates.
source: At P3 when Ptch1-LacZ + cells were visible in the dentate, the Msx2-Cre;Shhflx/flx;Ptch1-LacZ showed a third of the X-gal stained cells in the dentate compared to their heterozygous littermates (Figure 4A,A′).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 4A′.

claim: Cells expressing Sox2 marking dentate progenitor cells decreased in the P1 Msx2-Cre;Shhflx/flx mutants.
source: Cells expressing Sox2 marking dentate progenitor cells also decreased in the P1 mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: At P10 and P40, both radial glial and TACs were reduced in the Msx2-Cre;Shhflx/flx mutant.
source: At P10 and P40, both radial glial and TACs were reduced in the mutant.
evidence: This is shown and quantified in Figure 4C and C′.

claim: At P50, doublecortin (DCX)-positive immature dentate neurons were significantly reduced in the Msx2-Cre;Shhflx/flx mutants (p < 0.005).
source: At P50, doublecortin (DCX)-positive immature dentate neurons were also significantly reduced in the mutants (p < 0.005, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown and quantified in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 with statistical significance.

claim: Abundant GFP+;DAPI- cells were found near the calvarial suture and the dentate blood vessels in Gli1-CreERt2;Rosa-Yfp mice injected with TM at E15.5 and analyzed two days later.
source: To further examine hedgehog signaling and platelet formation, Gli1-CreERt2;Rosa-Yfp mice were injected with TM at E15.5 and analyzed two days later. Abundant GFP+;DAPI- cells were indeed found near the calvarial suture and the dentate blood vessels and the cells were CD42d + indicating that they are (pro)platelets (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A with CD42d staining.

claim: GFP+;DAPI- cells near the calvarial suture and dentate blood vessels were CD42d + indicating that they are (pro)platelets.
source: Abundant GFP+;DAPI- cells were indeed found near the calvarial suture and the dentate blood vessels and the cells were CD42d + indicating that they are (pro)platelets (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A with CD42d co-staining.

claim: GFP + cells in Gli1-CreERt2;Rosa-Yfp embryos were not stained with hematopoietic progenitor markers CD34 and CD45.
source: Hematopoietic progenitor markers such as CD34 and CD45 did not stain GFP + cells, while these cells were stained with platelet markers such as CD41, CD42d, and CD61 suggesting that platelets are generated from cells responsive to hedgehog signaling (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B with marker staining.

claim: GFP + cells in Gli1-CreERt2;Rosa-Yfp embryos were stained with platelet markers CD41, CD42d, and CD61.
source: Hematopoietic progenitor markers such as CD34 and CD45 did not stain GFP + cells, while these cells were stained with platelet markers such as CD41, CD42d, and CD61 suggesting that platelets are generated from cells responsive to hedgehog signaling (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B with marker staining.

claim: Platelets are generated from cells responsive to hedgehog signaling.
source: Hematopoietic progenitor markers such as CD34 and CD45 did not stain GFP + cells, while these cells were stained with platelet markers such as CD41, CD42d, and CD61 suggesting that platelets are generated from cells responsive to hedgehog signaling (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is inferred from the GFP+ platelet marker+ cells in Gli1 reporter mice.

claim: Platelets from E15.5 did not show Shh expression.
source: Platelets from E15.5 did not show Shh expression, but platelets from E17.5 embryonic blood showed strong Shh expression (Figure 7C,C′).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C by immunostaining of blood streaks.

claim: Platelets from E17.5 embryonic blood showed strong Shh expression.
source: Platelets from E15.5 did not show Shh expression, but platelets from E17.5 embryonic blood showed strong Shh expression (Figure 7C,C′).
evidence: This is shown and quantified in Figure 7C and C′.

claim: Western blot analysis of immunoprecipitates obtained with anti-CD41 antibodies using E17.5 embryonic blood samples showed that Shh precursors are present in platelets.
source: Western blot analysis of immunoprecipitates obtained with anti-CD41 antibodies using E17.5 embryonic blood samples to partially purify platelets showed that Shh precursors are present in platelets (Figure 7C″).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C″ by Western blot.

claim: Blood streaks from Krt14-Cre;Shh mutant embryos at E17.5 showed loss of Shh in the platelets.
source: To test this possibility, blood streaks from Krt14-Cre;Shh mutant embryos at E17.5 were used to detect Shh and we found loss of Shh in the platelets from the mutant embryonic blood supporting the idea that platelets take up Shh from dermal sources (Figure 7D,D′).
evidence: This is shown and quantified in Figure 7D and D′.

claim: Platelets take up Shh from dermal sources.
source: blood streaks from Krt14-Cre;Shh mutant embryos at E17.5 were used to detect Shh and we found loss of Shh in the platelets from the mutant embryonic blood supporting the idea that platelets take up Shh from dermal sources (Figure 7D,D′).
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of Shh in platelets when dermal Shh is deleted.

claim: Shh gene expression was not detected in the platelets as determined by using Shh-Cre with Ai14 reporter mice.
source: Both results support that platelets contain SHH proteins, but Shh gene expression was not detected in the platelets as determined by using Shh-Cre with Ai14 reporter mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Microvesicles from conditioned media of P1 head skin epidermal cells contained unprocessed Shh proteins.
source: Since we specifically detected unprocessed Shh proteins from our immunoprecipitation experiments, we cultivated epidermal cells from the P1 head skin to collect microvesicles from the conditioned media. The microvesicles from the conditioned media contained unprocessed Shh proteins as compared from the Shh produced in the cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4 by Western blot.

claim: Hair follicular Shh can be released as unprocessed form in microvesicles to be taken up by carrier cells such as platelets.
source: this result implies that hair follicular Shh can be released as unprocessed form in microvesicles to be taken up by carrier cells such as platelets.
evidence: This is inferred from the detection of unprocessed Shh in microvesicles.

claim: Nfe2−/− mutants showed reduced numbers of platelets in the dentate and the dermal cells adjacent to the HFs at P1.
source: Nfe2−/− mutants showed reduced numbers of platelets in the dentate and the dermal cells adjacent to the HFs at P1 (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A by CD41 staining.

claim: Blood streaks from P1 Nfe2 mutant showed that Shh+;CD41 + platelets were reduced to about 30% of normal.
source: Blood streaks from P1 Nfe2 mutant also showed that Shh+;CD41 + platelets were reduced to about 30% of normal (Figure 8A,A′).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 8A′.

claim: At E16.5, the number of Ki67 + dentate progenitors was not changed in Nfe2−/− mutants.
source: At E16.5, the number of Ki67 + dentate progenitors was not changed (Figure 8B,B′)
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 8B′ showing no significant difference.

claim: Ki67 + or Lef1+ dentate progenitors at P1 and Ki67 + dentate progenitors at P3 were significantly reduced in the Nfe2−/− mutants.
source: however, we found that the Ki67 + or Lef1+ dentate progenitors at P1 and Ki67 + dentate progenitors at P3 were significantly reduced in the Nfe2−/− mutants (Figure 8B′,C,D,D′).
evidence: This is shown and quantified in Figure 8B′, D, and D′ with statistical significance.

claim: At P3, the Ptch1-LacZ + cells were reduced to 50% in Nfe2−/−;Ptch1-LacZ mutants.
source: At P3, the Ptch1-LacZ + cells were reduced to 50% (Figure 8E,E′).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 8E′.

claim: The expression of Gli1-GFP + DG progenitors and their descendants in Nfe2−/− mutant pups at P1 were reduced to about 50%.
source: Consistent with this result, the expression of Gli1-GFP + DG progenitors and their descendants in Nfe2−/− mutant pups at P1 were also reduced to about 50% (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effect on dentate progenitors in the Nfe2−/− mutant was still seen at P5.
source: The effect on dentate progenitors in the mutant was still seen at P5, which was the latest age for mutant survival (Figure 8F,F′).
evidence: This is shown and quantified in Figure 8F and F′.

claim: Platelets are important for generation of perinatal Shh-responding dentate cells.
source: These data are consistent with our hypothesis that platelets are important for generation of perinatal Shh-responding dentate cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the Nfe2 mutant data showing reduced Shh-responding cells with reduced platelets.

claim: At E17.5 and P1, the dentate blood vessels were leaky, with 70 KDa dye shedding into the adjacent cells.
source: At E17.5 and P1, the dentate blood vessels were leaky, with 70 KDa dye shedding into the adjacent cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A by dextran perfusion experiments.

claim: Hedgehog-responding dentate cells have endfeet wrapping blood vessels forming neurovascular units.
source: Staining the Cre reporter Rosa-Yfp revealed the blood vessels wrapped by endfeet of hedgehog-responding dentate cells (Figure 6B) suggesting the involvement of Shh-responsive dentate stem cells in the formation of the dentate BBB.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B by GFP and PECAM staining.

claim: Shh-responsive dentate stem cells are involved in the formation of the dentate BBB.
source: Staining the Cre reporter Rosa-Yfp revealed the blood vessels wrapped by endfeet of hedgehog-responding dentate cells (Figure 6B) suggesting the involvement of Shh-responsive dentate stem cells in the formation of the dentate BBB.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of Gli1+ cells wrapping blood vessels.

claim: Neuronal cells adjacent to GFP + dentate cells showed uptake of perfused cadaverine dyes released from the leaky blood vessels of the dentate at P5.
source: The neuronal cells adjacent to GFP + dentate cells showed uptake of perfused cadaverine dyes released from the leaky blood vessels of the dentate.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C by cadaverine perfusion.

claim: At P5, dentate blood vessels showed weaker integrity compared to blood vessels in CA1 pyramidal zone.
source: Perfusion of 70 KDa dyes into P5 pups also showed weak integrity of dentate blood vessels compared to blood vessels in CA1 pyramidal zone (Figure 6D,D′).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 6D′ showing significantly more dye leakage in DG than CA1.

claim: Staining for fibrinogen revealed strong expression in the dentate at E17.5 to P1.
source: Staining for fibrinogen revealed strong expression in the dentate at E17.5 to P1 suggesting possible involvement of platelets and their fragments in the dentate and maturation of the dentate BBB (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6E by fibrinogen staining.

claim: CD41 marker showed circulating megakaryocytes and platelets within the dermis and in the dentate blood vessels and dentate at P1.
source: A marker of platelets, CD41, showed circulating megakaryocytes and platelets within the dermis (Figure 6F, arrow) and in the dentate blood vessels and dentate at P1 (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6F by CD41 staining.

claim: Ptch1-LacZ expression was detected in the calvarial suture at P3.
source: Ptch1-LacZ expression in the calvarium is presented. Arrow indicates X-gal staining of Ptch1-LacZ in the calvarial suture.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Ptch1-LacZ expression was detected in the fronts of developing calvarial bones at P3.
source: Ptch1-LacZ expression was detected in the fronts of developing calvarial bones (arrows).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Hedgehog-responding cells in E17.5 Gli1-CreERt2;Rosa-Yfp embryos (TM at E15.5) were Pdgfrβ+ and overlapped with Vimentin+ and Desmin + perivascular cells.
source: A closer examination of the hedgehog-responding cells in sections of E17 Gli1-CreERt2;Rosa-Yfp embryos 48 hr after Tamoxifen induction revealed that GFP + cells were Pdgfrβ+ and overlapped with Vimentin+ and Desmin + perivascular cells (Figure 5C,C′).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and C′ by co-staining.

claim: Inhibition of dermal mesenchymal hedgehog signaling dramatically reduced the size of the skull at P3 in Pdgfrb-Cre;Smoflx/flx mutants.
source: Inhibition of dermal mesenchymal hedgehog signaling dramatically reduced the size of the skull at P3, which was not observed in either Krt14-Cre;Shhflx/flx and Msx2-Cre;Shhflx/flx mutants (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Pdgfrb-Cre;Smoflx/flx mutants showed a slight but smaller magnitude decrease in Ki67 + dentate progenitors at E17.5 and P1.
source: In these mutants, there was a slight but smaller magnitude decrease in Ki67 + dentate progenitors at E17.5 and P1 (Figure 5E,E′).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 5E′.

claim: The change in dentate progenitors in the Shh mutants, Krt14-Cre;Shhflx/flx and Msx2-Cre;Shhflx/flx was much greater than in Pdgfrb-Cre;Smoflx/flx mutants.
source: These results suggest that hedgehog signaling in dermal mesenchymal cells might mediate some role in dentate expansion; however, the change in dentate progenitors in the Shh mutants, Krt14-Cre;Shhflx/flx and Msx2-Cre;Shhflx/flx was much greater implying that an indirect role via mesenchymal cells and skull dysplasia isn't the primary explanation.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the magnitude of effects across different mutants.

claim: Disrupted neurogenesis is linked to multiple neurological and psychiatric diseases.
source: Neural stem cells in the dentate gyrus (DG) consistently provide new excitatory neurons to modulate hippocampal circuitry and disrupted neurogenesis is linked to multiple neurological and psychiatric diseases (Zhao et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Deletion of dorsal Shh expression using Emx1-Cre or NeuroD6-Cre resulted in only a modest effect on the cortex and more significant but postnatal effect in the DG.
source: However, deletion of dorsal Shh expression using Emx1-Cre or NeuroD6-Cre resulted in only a modest effect on the cortex and more significant but postnatal effect in the DG (Komada et al., 2008; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Platelets are thrombotic anuclear cell fragments that regulate hemostasis, wound healing, and tissue repair.
source: It is well known that platelets are thrombotic anuclear cell fragments that regulate hemostasis, wound healing, and tissue repair (Gawaz and Vogel, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Platelets are a source of various cytokines and growth factors including PDGF, HGF, VEGF, PAF, TGFβ1, and BDNF.
source: Growth factors from platelets have been known to promote growth of fibroblasts, hepatocytes, glial cells, hippocampal neurons, and endothelial cells, and platelets are the best source of purifying growth factors such as PDGF, HGF, VEGF, PAF, TGFβ1, and BDNF (Kohler and Lipton, 1974; Westermark and Wasteson, 1976; Nakamura et al., 1986; Miyazono et al., 1988; Clark et al., 1992; Mohle et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Meis1 mutant embryos lack platelets and show defective separation of blood and lymphatic vessels.
source: Meis1 mutant embryos lack platelets and show defective separation of blood and lymphatic vessels, while CLEC-2 receptors on platelets regulate lymphatic endothelial SLP-76 signaling and specify the lymphatic vessels from the blood vessels (Bertozzi et al., 2010; Carramolino et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: CLEC-2 receptors on platelets regulate lymphatic endothelial SLP-76 signaling and specify the lymphatic vessels from the blood vessels.
source: Meis1 mutant embryos lack platelets and show defective separation of blood and lymphatic vessels, while CLEC-2 receptors on platelets regulate lymphatic endothelial SLP-76 signaling and specify the lymphatic vessels from the blood vessels (Bertozzi et al., 2010; Carramolino et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: In stroke, platelet lysates injected into the ventricle showed a neuroprotective effect with increases in neurogenesis and angiogenesis.
source: In a pathological condition like stroke, platelet lysates injected into the ventricle showed a neuroprotective effect with increases in neurogenesis and angiogenesis (Hayon et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Proliferation of adult dentate stem cells proceeds in perivascular microenvironments.
source: Proliferation of adult dentate stem cells proceeds in perivascular microenvironements (Palmer et al., 2000)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Youthful systemic circulation rejuvenates aged stem cells in heterochronic-aged parabionts.
source: Recent studies showing that youthful systemic circulation rejuvenates aged stem cells in heterochronic-aged parabionts provides a fascinating additional implication of our study (Conboy et al., 2005; Villeda et al., 2011; Conboy and Rando, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.
